patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Minnesota → India: Fr Joseph Jeyapaul (returned by extradition 2014); Phoenix → Rome: Joseph Henn (fugitive 2003–2019); Scranton (USA) → Ciudad del Este (Paraguay): Fr Carlos Urrutigoity; Tehuacán → Los Angeles → Mexico: Fr Nicolás Aguilar Rivera; Ireland → United States: Fr Brendan Smyth; Birmingham → California: Fr James Robinson; Vancouver → Long Island, New York: Fr Damian Cooper.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Jeffrey Epstein: first report 1996, first action 2006 (10 years). Maria Farmer reported to the FBI in 1996 with no known action; after the 2005 Palm Beach police probe, the 2007 federal non-prosecution agreement ended the federal case and he served 13 months in a county stockade on a state plea (2008). Federal sex-trafficking charges came only in July 2019 after the Miami Herald series (2018) Larry Nassar: first report 1997, first action 2016 (19 years). Athletes complained from 1997, including to MSU coach Kathie Klages; USA Gymnastics told 17 June 2015 and FBI in July 2015, but the FBI did not act; DOJ IG (2021) found at least 70 more athletes abused between FBI reports and his arrest Jerry Sandusky (Penn State): first report 1998, first action 2011 (13 years). A 1998 report to Penn State police was not prosecuted; a 2001 eyewitness report by Mike McQueary went to Paterno and university leaders, who did not report to police (Freeh report, 2012) Theodore McCarrick: first report 1994, first action 2018 (24 years). A priest wrote to Bishop Hughes in 1994; the nuncio was warned in 1994; further warnings including to Benedict XVI (2008); McCarrick denied them to the Vatican and was made a cardinal in 2001 R. Kelly: first report 2000, first action 2019 (19 years). Chicago Sun-Times investigated from August 2000; 2002 child-pornography prosecution ended in acquittal in 2008 Mark Foley (House pages): first report 2000, first action 2006 (6 years). patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role: Lobbying against reform and bankruptcy filings
patterns.role_note: At least 41 Catholic dioceses and orders, the Boy Scouts and USA Gymnastics filed for bankruptcy facing abuse claims; Catholic, insurance and Scouts lobbying against limitation reform is documented in several states.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2002: USCCB National Review Board / John Jay College study, report Feb 2004. 10,667 allegations; 4,392 clergy accused (about 4% of 109,694 clergy)
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Msgr Carlo Alberto Capella, Holy See nunciature in Washington: Convicted by a Vatican tribunal 2018: five years and a €5,000 fine — not tried in the US or Canada
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 3,137 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–) (receiving or involved). United States — Indian Adoption Project (1958–67) and the Indian Child Welfare Act 1978. Federal Indian Boarding Schools — Interior Department investigation. United States — 'Baby Scoop Era' adoptions of unmarried mothers' babies (1945–1973).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2003: PROTECT Act (30 April 2003): US citizens/residents prosecutable for illicit sexual conduct abroad with under-18s whether or not they intended it before travel; maximum raised to 30 years. ICE "Operation Predator" (2003) led to over 11,000 arrests incl. more than 1,100 outside the US 2016: International Megan's Law signed 8 Feb 2016; from 31 Oct 2017 passports of covered offenders carry a unique identifier; 21-day advance notice of foreign travel; Angel Watch notifies destination countries
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Police ran abuse sites to catch users
patterns.role_note: Playpen / Operation Pacifier — FBI ran the site for 13 days (police ran abuse sites to catch users). Claims that Epstein was tied to intelligence services (claimed, not established).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 49,021 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (16% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: United States — Indian Adoption Project (1958–67) and the Indian Child Welfare Act 1978; United States — Georgia Tann / Tennessee Children's Home Society black-market adoptions; Federal Indian Boarding Schools — Interior Department investigation; Los Angeles County juvenile halls and MacLaren Children's Center — $4bn settlement; New Hampshire Youth Development Center, Manchester; US juvenile facilities — BJS National Survey of Youth in Custody 2018; Texas foster care — federal court finds 'rape and over-medication were the norm'; Epstein — Palm Beach police investigation and 2006 state charge; Epstein — 2007 federal non-prosecution agreement and 2008 state plea; Epstein — 2019 federal sex-trafficking indictment and death in custody; Ghislaine Maxwell — convicted of sex trafficking of a minor; Zorro Ranch, New Mexico — state probe dropped in 2019, reopened 2026; Epstein Files Transparency.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No national inquiry into institutional abuse found
patterns.role_note: Investigations have been state-level (attorneys general, grand juries) and church-commissioned
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: False alarms that drown real cases
patterns.role_note: Franklin credit union 'child prostitution ring' allegations, Nebraska. 'Pizzagate' — false claim of a child-trafficking ring at a Washington pizzeria. McMartin preschool trial — 'satanic abuse' panic ends in acquittals.
patterns.pattern_summary: False stories about child trafficking take police time and public attention away from real cases. In July 2020 a claim spread online that the furniture company Wayfair was selling children through its listings. The US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about it within days, and Polaris, the charity that runs the hotline, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed help; none of the reports contained new information. In 2016 a false claim known as "Pizzagate", that a Washington pizza restaurant was the centre of a child-abuse ring, led a man to fire a rifle inside the restaurant. In London, the Metropolitan Police spent more than £2 million on Operation Midland, which investigated claims made by Carl Beech about a ring of powerful men; the claims were false, Beech was jailed for perverting the course of justice, and he had separately admitted child sexual offences. In the 1980s the McMartin preschool case in California, built on claims of ritual abuse, cost about $14 million and ended without a conviction.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–)
cases.who: Chilean state agencies, hospital and social-service staff, intermediaries
cases.what: Children were taken from mainly poor mothers, some told their babies had died, and sent for adoption to families in the United States and Europe, including Sweden; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990). A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. A congressional committee concluded the state was responsible; as of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. Sweden opened its own investigation into intercountry adoptions after activism by Chilean adoptees.

cases.title: Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007)
cases.who: Private notaries (notarios), baby brokers, foster homes, officials
cases.what: After the civil war ended in 1996, adoptions abroad rose each year, run almost entirely (about 98%) by private notaries who handled both sides without court review and charged $35,000 or more per child; 97% of children went to the US. CICIG's 2010 report studied 153 cases and found 78% violated the new law in some way. Guatemala passed a Hague-compliant law on 11 December 2007 and stopped new adoptions to the US from 1 January 2008; the US State Department announced on 9 January 2008 it would not allow new adoptions until procedures were compliant.

cases.title: United States — Georgia Tann / Tennessee Children's Home Society black-market adoptions
cases.who: Tennessee Children's Home Society (Shelby County branch) under Georgia Tann
cases.what: From 1924 to 1950 Georgia Tann used the Memphis branch of the Tennessee Children's Home Society to take children from poor families and sell them, charging up to $5,000 for out-of-state adoptions when Tennessee adoptions cost about $7. A state investigation into adoption fraud led to the home's closure in 1950; Tann died before its findings were published.

cases.title: South Korea — Brothers Home children sent overseas for adoption
cases.who: Brothers Home (Busan detention facility); receiving agencies named by AP incl. Holt International, Children's Home Society of Minnesota
cases.what: Brothers Home was a state-backed facility where people deemed vagrants were confined and forced to work; the TRC recognised state culpability on 23 August 2022 and counted 657 deaths there 1975–1988. An AP investigation (November 2019) found Brothers Home organised the adoption of 19 children abroad in 1979–1986 and that six US agencies received children from it. In February 2025 the TRC confirmed at least 31 children were improperly sent overseas for adoption through the facility.

cases.title: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
cases.who: Salvadoran armed forces
cases.what: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cases.cover_up: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.

cases.title: US juvenile facilities — BJS National Survey of Youth in Custody 2018
cases.who: State and locally run juvenile detention and correctional facilities
cases.what: The Bureau of Justice Statistics surveyed 6,049 youth in 327 juvenile facilities between March and December 2018. 7.1% reported sexual victimisation in the previous 12 months, and 5.8% reported sexual misconduct by staff (down from 7.7% in 2012). Youth-on-youth forced or coerced victimisation was reported by 1.9%.

cases.title: Texas foster care — federal court finds 'rape and over-medication were the norm'
cases.who: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services; Health and Human Services Commission
cases.what: In a class action filed in 2011 on behalf of children in long-term state care, US District Judge Janis Graham Jack ruled in December 2015 that Texas violated foster children's constitutional rights by placing them in a system where 'rape and over-medication were the norm'. She later ordered 24-hour awake supervision and flagging of children who were victims or perpetrators of sexual violence. In April 2024 she found the state in contempt for a third time and fined it $100,000 a day over failures to investigate abuse reports.
cases.cover_up: Judge Jack held Texas in contempt three times (2019, 2020, April 2024) for failing to investigate abuse complaints and protect children; in 2019 she said she could no longer find the department credible.

cases.title: Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017
cases.who: Afghan National Defense and Security Forces and Afghan Local Police commanders; US military chain of command
cases.what: In September 2015 The New York Times reported that US soldiers had been told to ignore sexual abuse of boys by Afghan allies, describing it as rampant; nearly 100 members of Congress then asked the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR) to investigate. SIGAR's report, sent to Congress in 2017 and made public on 23 January 2018, found that as of August 2016 the Pentagon was tracking 75 gross human rights violations by Afghan security forces from 2010 to 2016, at least seven of them child sexual assault, and said 'the full extent of child sexual assault committed by Afghan security forces may never be known'. The Pentagon used the 'notwithstanding' exception to the Leahy Law to keep supporting implicated units, including approving continued funding in December 2015 for 12 units implicated in 14 violations.
cases.cover_up: NYT (2015) reported US soldiers were instructed not to intervene, in some cases even on US bases; US law (Leahy) required cutting aid to offending units but SIGAR/NYT reported that never happened. Capt. Dan Quinn was relieved and Sgt 1st Class Charles Martland initially separated after beating an ALP commander who admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy (2011).

cases.title: Zorro Ranch, New Mexico — state probe dropped in 2019, reopened 2026
cases.who: Jeffrey Epstein; New Mexico law enforcement
cases.what: Epstein bought the 7,600-acre ranch in 1993. New Mexico AG Raúl Torrez reopened a criminal investigation on 12 March 2026 citing previously sealed FBI files, and state officials searched the ranch in March 2026 with the new owners' cooperation. A four-member legislative truth commission created in the 2026 session released a 119-page interim report on 5 Aug 2026; a final report is due by end of 2026. Allegations that bodies were buried near the ranch, raised in the files, are unconfirmed.
cases.cover_up: The state AG's 2019 investigation was closed at the request of the US Attorney's Office (SDNY). The 2026 interim commission report found Epstein likely got 'preferential treatment' from New Mexico law enforcement, avoided sex-offender registration via a loophole, and used NDAs, secrecy protocols and a $7m-a-year payroll to keep activity out of view. The FBI never searched the ranch in 2019.

cases.title: Epstein Files Transparency Act and DOJ releases (2025–2026)
cases.who: US Department of Justice; FBI; House Oversight Committee
cases.what: A 7 July 2025 DOJ/FBI memo said there was no incriminating 'client list', no credible evidence that Epstein blackmailed prominent people, and that his death was suicide; it also said Epstein 'harmed over one thousand victims'. Congress then passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act 427–1 in the House and by unanimous consent in the Senate, and it was signed on 19 Nov 2025. DOJ began releasing files on 19 Dec 2025 and on 30 Jan 2026 published over 3 million more pages (about 3.5 million in total), saying notable individuals were not redacted and warning that the release may include fake or false material submitted by the public. On 5 Mar 2026, after an NPR investigation found pages had been withheld, DOJ published 16 more pages. The releases documented Epstein's continued contact with prominent people after 2008 and led to police inquiries and resignations abroad; they did not establish a client list.
cases.cover_up: DOJ said it identified about 6 million potentially responsive pages but released about 3.5 million, withholding about 200,000 under privilege, abuse material and victim-identity grounds; critics in both parties said it broke the law. Faulty redactions exposed at least 43 victims' names (WSJ). The DOJ Inspector General opened a compliance review in April 2026.

cases.title: Mark Foley — messages to congressional pages; House leadership 'negligent'
cases.who: Rep. Mark Foley; House Republican leadership
cases.what: In late September 2006 sexually suggestive emails and instant messages from Rep. Mark Foley to teenage boys who had served as House pages became public; he resigned on 29 Sept 2006. On 8 Dec 2006 the House Ethics Committee found Republican members and staff had been negligent in handling earlier warnings about his conduct but that no House rules were broken, and recommended no punishment. No criminal charges were brought; Florida's state investigation was closed in September 2008 citing insufficient evidence.
cases.cover_up: Complaints reached House staff and leaders around 2000–2005. The House Ethics Committee (Dec 2006) found Speaker Hastert and other leaders 'negligent' but recommended no sanctions. Florida's FDLE closed its probe in 2008 citing insufficient evidence and said Congress and Foley denied it access to data.

cases.title: Cambodia — Lauryn Galindo adoption-fraud conspiracy; US moratorium 2001
cases.who: US facilitator Lauryn Galindo and associates; Cambodian officials paid by facilitators
cases.what: The US imposed a moratorium on Cambodian adoptions in late 2001 after fraudulent cases and raids by the Cambodian rights group LICADHO. Facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions for US families in 1997–2001, more than half of all Cambodian adoptions; the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for babies. In 2004 she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering in 17 cases, admitting she falsified documents that erased children's identities (she denied trafficking), and faced an 18-month sentence. Some adoptive families later found their children had living relatives.

cases.title: Marshall Islands — Paul Petersen 'baby mill' adoption scheme
cases.who: Paul Petersen, Maricopa County (Arizona) Assessor and adoption lawyer
cases.what: Petersen, an elected Arizona official, paid recruiters to bring pregnant Marshallese women to the US, paying them about $10,000 to give up their babies and charging adoptive couples about $35,000, although the Compact of Free Association bars Marshallese travel to the US for adoption. Charged in October 2019 in Utah, Arizona and Arkansas, he pleaded guilty in all three courts in June 2020 (human smuggling, fraud, communication fraud) and was sentenced in December 2020 in federal court in Arkansas to more than six years in prison. He also fraudulently obtained about $814,000 in Arizona Medicaid funds for the women.

cases.title: Okinawa — rape of a 12-year-old girl by three US servicemen (1995)
cases.who: US Navy and Marine Corps personnel from Camp Hansen
cases.what: In September 1995 three US servicemen based on Okinawa abducted and raped a 12-year-old Okinawan schoolgirl. They were tried in a Japanese court and in 1996 were each found guilty and sentenced to between six years and six months and seven years in prison. The case triggered mass protests against the US bases.

cases.title: Epstein — Palm Beach police investigation and 2006 state charge
cases.who: Jeffrey Epstein (financier)
cases.what: In March 2005 a woman told Palm Beach police her 14-year-old stepdaughter had been paid to give Epstein a massage at his mansion. A 13-month police investigation identified about 35 girls. In July 2006 a state grand jury returned a single count of felony solicitation of prostitution and Epstein was arrested on 23 July 2006. Reiter later called the outcome 'the worst failure of the criminal justice system' in modern times.
cases.cover_up: Police chief Michael Reiter said state prosecutors under State Attorney Barry Krischer grew dismissive about six months in; he asked Krischer to step aside. The July 2006 state grand jury returned only one felony solicitation-of-prostitution count. Reiter then referred the case to the FBI.

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.name: Focus on Children (Utah)
networks.what: Agency run by Scott and Karen Banks that arranged about 80 adoptions of Samoan children whose parents were told it was temporary schooling; the defendants pleaded guilty in January 2009 and were banned from adoption work.

networks.name: European Adoption Consultants (Ohio)
networks.what: Defunct Ohio agency that, per a 2020 federal indictment, procured more than 30 Ugandan children for US clients in 2013–2016 through bribery of Ugandan officials, and arranged a fraudulent Polish adoption. One employee pleaded guilty in 2019; others were charged in 2020.

networks.name: New Life Children's Refuge (Idaho)
networks.what: Baptist group whose ten members were arrested on 29 January 2010 taking 33 Haitian children to the Dominican Republic; leader Laura Silsby was convicted of arranging irregular travel.

networks.name: Federal Indian boarding school system (US)
networks.what: 417 federal Indian boarding schools in 37 states or territories, 1819–1969, documented by the Department of the Interior with at least 973 child deaths and physical, sexual and emotional abuse.

networks.name: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
networks.what: National Scout associations; the Boy Scouts of America faced more than 82,000 sexual abuse claims in its 2020 bankruptcy and had kept internal 'ineligible volunteer' files on suspected abusers.

networks.name: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
networks.what: A recurring pattern in which orphanages are set up or kept full to attract foreign donations, volunteers and tourists, recruiting children who mostly have living parents, sometimes with payments to families or forged documents. Governments and the US State Department have recognised it as trafficking, and Australia's parliament classed it as modern slavery in 2017.

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Minnesota → India: Fr Joseph Jeyapaul (returned by extradition 2014).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Muzaffarpur shelter home: first report 2018, first action 2018 (0 years). Operator Brajesh Thakur was politically connected; TISS social audit (report April 2018) exposed abuse; minister Manju Verma resigned; CBI later cleared her despite call records showing contact with Thakur Asaram Bapu: first report 2013, first action 2013 (0 years). Witnesses were attacked: a former aide shot dead May 2014; key Surat witness shot dead January 2015 Unnao rape case (MLA Kuldeep Singh Sengar): first report 2017, first action 2018 (1 years). The victim's father died in police custody; arrest came only after the Allahabad High Court ordered it Bishop Franco Mulakkal (acquitted): first report 2018, first action 2018 (0 years). A nun's June 2018 complaint alleged 13 rapes 2014-2016; arrested only on 21 Sept 2018 after protests by nuns
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: No national inquiry into institutional abuse found. Scholars note allegations "often remain informal and rarely progress to formal charges" (Matthew N. Schmalz)
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Nithyananda: Fugitive
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 12,511 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 2001: scandal: Andhra Pradesh adoption racket (Tender Loving Care Home) exposed, March 2001 2005: ban: Andhra Pradesh bars private agencies from placing children; 10 convicted (31 August) 2005: scandal: Chennai police arrest 9 over Malaysian Social Services kidnapping-for-adoption case (May) 2008: freeze: Australia freezes adoptions through Indian agencies whose conduct was in doubt (2 September)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: India — Preet Mandir, Pune: CBI case on inter-country adoption racket; Muzaffarpur shelter home — TISS audit and convictions; TISS 'Koshish' social audit of 110 Bihar children's homes; Deoria shelter home, Uttar Pradesh — girls rescued, CBI case; Unnao rape case — MLA Kuldeep Singh Sengar.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found South Asia lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation. Scholars note allegations "often remain informal and rarely progress to formal charges" (Matthew N. Schmalz)
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: TISS 'Koshish' social audit of 110 Bihar children's homes
cases.who: Children's and girls' homes funded by the Bihar Social Welfare Department, many NGO-run
cases.what: At the Bihar government's request, the Koshish unit of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences visited 110 children's homes in 38 districts and submitted its audit to the Social Welfare Department on 27 April 2018, grading homes as better, administrative negligence or criminal negligence. The Muzaffarpur girls' home run by Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti was graded criminal negligence, and the report raised harassment or abuse at 14 other homes, including a girls' home with complaints of severe sexual harassment and violence and homes where children were routinely beaten. The audit triggered the Muzaffarpur FIR of 31 May 2018 and later CBI cases against other Bihar shelter homes.
cases.cover_up: In the audited Bhagalpur home staff refused to give the audit team the key to the complaint box, saying it was lost; the department's director evaded questions about action on the other 14 homes.

cases.title: Muzaffarpur shelter home — TISS audit and convictions
cases.who: Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti (state-funded NGO run by Brajesh Thakur); Bihar Social Welfare Department
cases.what: A social audit of Bihar shelter homes by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, submitted in April 2018, flagged sexual abuse at the Muzaffarpur girls' home run by Brajesh Thakur's NGO; an FIR followed on 31 May 2018. Medical examination indicated sexual abuse of 34 girls, most of them children. The Supreme Court took up the case and, at the CBI's request, transferred the trial to a POCSO court at Saket, Delhi, because the accused were influential in Bihar. On 20 January 2020 that court convicted Thakur and 18 others; Thakur was sentenced to life imprisonment and has appealed.
cases.cover_up: The then district child protection officer was among the accused; Bihar Social Welfare Minister Manju Verma resigned over the case; the Supreme Court criticised the state for funding the NGO and moved the trial to Delhi. CBI cleared Verma and her husband, a finding disputed by The Caravan.

cases.title: Unnao rape case — MLA Kuldeep Singh Sengar
cases.who: Kuldeep Singh Sengar (BJP MLA, Uttar Pradesh)
cases.what: Sengar, then a BJP MLA in Uttar Pradesh, was convicted in December 2019 by a special CBI court in Delhi of raping a minor girl in Unnao district in 2017, and sentenced to life imprisonment; the BJP had expelled him. In December 2025 the Delhi High Court suspended his sentence; on 29 Dec 2025 the Supreme Court stayed that order on the CBI's appeal, and in May 2026 it set the suspension aside, directing the High Court to decide his appeal against conviction within three months or pass a fresh order.
cases.cover_up: The victim's father died in police custody; in July 2019 a truck crash killed two of her aunts and critically injured her and her lawyer (a court later accepted the CBI finding of no foul play in the crash). The arrest came only after the Allahabad High Court ordered it in 2018.

cases.title: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
cases.who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
cases.what: Swiss authorities soon realised that the placement of children for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, was also driven by economic interests and linked to organised child trafficking; decisions were often made on incomplete or falsified documents, and checks on foster families and on legal requirements were insufficient. From the 2010s, under pressure from groups such as Back to the Roots, intercountry adoptions from Tibet, Sri Lanka and India drew public attention. In 2018 the Federal Assembly commissioned a study on intercountry adoption; the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

cases.title: India — Preet Mandir, Pune: CBI case on inter-country adoption racket
cases.who: Preet Mandir adoption agency; state officials
cases.what: Preet Mandir placed 518 children in 2004–2006, most abroad, and Frontline reported in 2005 it handled about 7% of India's foreign adoptions while charging high 'donation' fees. CNN-IBN reported in December 2007 that the CBI had confirmed findings on illegal adoptions. On 18 May 2010 the CBI registered a case against a managing trustee and state officials over an alleged inter-country adoption racket.

cases.title: Deoria shelter home, Uttar Pradesh — girls rescued, CBI case
cases.who: Maa Vindhyavasini Mahila Prashikshan Evam Samaj Sewa Sansthan (NGO); director Girija Tripathi and superintendent Kanchan Lata Tripathi
cases.what: The case came to light when a 10-year-old girl escaped to a women's police station and said girls were taken away in cars in the afternoons and returned crying in the morning. Police rescued 24 girls on 5 August 2018 and sealed the home. Police charge-sheeted the director and her daughter, and seven others in a second FIR. In 2019 the CBI took over and registered cases including sexual harassment, human trafficking, sexual assault and adoption without legal procedure.
cases.cover_up: The UP Women and Child Development Minister said the NGO's recognition had been revoked and funds stopped a year earlier, yet it continued to operate; the government said it would examine who was responsible.

cases.title: Nepal → India — trafficking of girls to Indian brothels (estimates)
cases.who: Trafficking networks recruiting via false job, marriage and online romance offers
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers use job offers and online romance scams to recruit Nepali women and children to India for sex trafficking; Nepali courts convicted 406 traffickers (231 for sex trafficking) in the year. A 2024 study it cites found a majority of workers in Nepal's adult entertainment sector were sex-trafficking victims, nearly half of them children. Research collated on Wikipedia gives estimates of 5,000–10,000 Nepali women and girls trafficked to India each year across a 1,850 km open border.
cases.cover_up: US TIP 2025: serious concerns of official complicity; traffickers bribe some Indian officials to fly Nepali workers to third countries.

cases.title: Bangladesh — girls trafficked to India, Pakistan and the Gulf; Rohingya girls near Cox's Bazar (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers, recruitment agents, armed groups in Rohingya camps
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Bangladeshi women and girls in sex trafficking abroad, including in India, Pakistan and Gulf countries, and observers estimate children are 40 per cent of Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims exploited abroad. Tourists have increased demand for sexual exploitation, including of Rohingya girls, near Cox's Bazar, where more than one million Rohingya refugees live in 33 camps. Courts convicted 103 traffickers, down from 407.
cases.cover_up: Corruption and official complicity were significant concerns; corrupt policing in Rohingya camps.

cases.title: Devadasi dedication of girls — Karnataka and neighbouring states
cases.who: Temple dedication practice (mostly Dalit girls)
cases.what: Girls, mostly from Dalit families, are dedicated to temple deities and then sexually exploited, despite laws against the practice, including Karnataka's 1982 ban. The Karnataka government's last survey, in 2008, counted 40,600 devadasis; NGOs and a 2018 Karnataka State Women's University study found more than 80,000. Girls as young as seven have been pushed into the tradition.

cases.title: India — Andhra Pradesh adoption racket (Tender Loving Care Home)
cases.who: St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home and other agencies
cases.what: On 22 March 2001 Hyderabad police arrested a man carrying three baby girls allegedly bound for St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home; other agencies were also flagged. A chargesheet said the home earned Rs 3.33 crore from intercountry adoptions, mainly to the US, in 1999–2001. On 31 August 2005 Sister Teresa Maria Kattikaran and nine others were sentenced to six months' imprisonment for cheating and forgery, and Andhra Pradesh became the first state to bar private agencies from placing children.

cases.title: Apna Ghar shelter, Rohtak — CBI court convictions
cases.who: Apna Ghar, a government-funded shelter run by Jaswanti Devi and relatives
cases.what: The case began in 2012 when three girls escaped from the government-funded Apna Ghar shelter and told police residents were physically and sexually abused and used as bonded labour. The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights raided it in May 2012; Haryana sealed it in June 2012 and the CBI charge-sheeted ten people in August 2012. On 18 April 2018 a special CBI court in Panchkula convicted nine, including of rape, abortion without consent, bonded labour and offences under the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act and Juvenile Justice Act; on 27 April 2018 Jaswanti Devi, her son-in-law and a driver were sentenced to life. A former child development project officer who oversaw the shelter was acquitted.

cases.title: Fr Joseph Jeyapaul — Indian priest extradited to Minnesota
cases.who: Diocese of Crookston, Minnesota; diocese in India
cases.what: An Indian priest serving in the Diocese of Crookston in 2004–2005 was removed from ministry in September 2005 and returned to India. He was charged in 2006 with raping a girl from age 14; extradition took about five years after an Interpol alert, with arrest in Erode, India in 2012 and return to Minnesota in November 2014. In 2015 he pleaded guilty to criminal sexual misconduct involving a teenage girl and was sentenced to a year and a day (time served); the rape charges were dismissed under the plea deal and he faced deportation to India.
cases.cover_up: The Vatican recommended his removal from the priesthood, but the Indian bishop instead imposed a year in a monastery through a canonical trial, and he continued as a priest in India.

cases.title: ISKCON boarding schools (gurukulas) — acknowledged abuse
cases.who: International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON)
cases.what: In the 1990s ISKCON leaders acknowledged physical, emotional and sexual abuse of children in the movement's boarding schools in the US and India in the 1970s and 1980s, and in 1998 ISKCON itself published an exposé. A $900 million lawsuit filed in Texas in 2002 (the Turley case) led ISKCON temples into Chapter 11 bankruptcy and a $15 million settlement in 2008. ISKCON then set up a Child Protection Office.

cases.title: India — Malaysian Social Services, Chennai: children kidnapped for adoption
cases.who: Malaysian Social Services adoption agency
cases.what: Police suspected the family running the Malaysian Social Services agency since 1991 of kidnapping and trafficking more than 350 children; in May 2005 Chennai police arrested three family members and six others. Children allegedly had their appearance changed and histories fabricated; officers found files for 120 children sent overseas. TIME reported in 2008 that Australian authorities had earlier warnings.

cases.title: Kolkata red-light areas — rescues of trafficked Nepali girls and minors (2015, 2025)
cases.who: Brothel keepers and traffickers in Kolkata
cases.what: In January 2015 police, with International Justice Mission and three NGOs, freed six young women trafficked from Nepal from four brothels in Kolkata's largest red-light area; all had fake adult ID documents, which IJM said traffickers issue to underage girls. On 10 September 2025 Kolkata Police's Anti-Human Trafficking Unit rescued ten people including nine minor girls from a house in Burtolla, North Kolkata, and arrested six people, including the couple running it (charged). The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers recruit significant numbers of Nepali and Bangladeshi women and girls for sex trafficking in India.

cases.title: 'Sweetie' sting — 20,000 offers to pay for webcam abuse
cases.who: Terre des hommes Netherlands (virtual 10-year-old 'Sweetie')
cases.what: In a 10-week investigation run from a warehouse in Amsterdam, Terre des hommes Netherlands posed in public chatrooms as 'Sweetie', a computer-generated 10-year-old Filipina girl, to show the scale of webcam child sex abuse: 20,000 internet users offered to pay for webcam sex performances. The researchers identified about 1,000 of them, from 65 countries, including 110 in the UK and 254 traced to computers in the US, and on 4 November 2013 handed their details to Interpol. They said online child exploitation had become a hardened criminal industry in the Philippines.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Asaram Bapu ashrams
networks.what: Network of ashrams and gurukuls; founder Asaram convicted in 2018 of raping a 16-year-old and in 2023 in a Surat sisters' case. Two boys died at the Motera gurukul in 2008; an inquiry blamed ashram negligence.

networks.name: International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON)
networks.what: Acknowledged abuse in its boarding schools in the 1970s–80s; $15 million settlement in 2008.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role: Welfare state, church and unmarried mothers
patterns.role_note: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2013: Korean Institute of Criminology (Jan 2013): South Korean men are the primary market for child sex tourism in Southeast Asia
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: South Korea — Brothers Home children sent overseas for adoption
cases.who: Brothers Home (Busan detention facility); receiving agencies named by AP incl. Holt International, Children's Home Society of Minnesota
cases.what: Brothers Home was a state-backed facility where people deemed vagrants were confined and forced to work; the TRC recognised state culpability on 23 August 2022 and counted 657 deaths there 1975–1988. An AP investigation (November 2019) found Brothers Home organised the adoption of 19 children abroad in 1979–1986 and that six US agencies received children from it. In February 2025 the TRC confirmed at least 31 children were improperly sent overseas for adoption through the facility.

cases.title: France — state report finds 'illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption
cases.who: French government and adoption associations
cases.what: In March 2024 France released an assessment acknowledging that its government had long known of 'the existence of illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption, and that diplomatic and association archives showed these practices existed in countries over long periods. France received 11,165 Korean children 1968–2008 among others.
cases.cover_up: The report said public authorities were alerted early, including at the highest levels, and were late in taking action.

cases.title: Norway — state investigation of illegal intercountry adoptions (2023–)
cases.who: Norwegian state; private adoption organisations
cases.what: Norway launched an investigation in 2023 into whether illegal or unethical practices occurred in intercountry adoptions and whether Norwegian officials failed to control them; the foreign ministry said it was 'aware of serious findings' (AP, 2024). Norway received 6,295 Korean children 1955–2008, and in 1974–75 Scandinavian diplomats pressed South Korea to keep sending children after it tried to stop. In September 2025 a Korean-born adoptee served notice of a lawsuit against the Norwegian state alleging her adoption was illegal (allegation).

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Gwangju Inhwa School for the deaf — the 'Dogani' case
cases.who: Gwangju Inhwa School for deaf students (founded 1961; principal was the founder's son)
cases.what: A 2005 investigation found that six people at the school, including the headmaster, had sexually harassed or raped at least nine deaf students from 2000 onward. Four received prison terms, two of which were later suspended; two escaped punishment because the statute of limitations had expired. After the 2011 film 'Silenced' (Dogani), police opened a new investigation, the city moved to close the school in November 2011, and on 28 Oct 2011 the National Assembly passed the 'Dogani Law' removing the statute of limitations for sex crimes against children under 13 and disabled people. In July 2012 a former administrator was sentenced to 12 years for sexually assaulting an 18-year-old student in April 2005.
cases.cover_up: The teacher who alerted human rights groups in 2005 was fired; police acted only four months later after former students went to national TV; the city government and school board passed the case back and forth; appeal courts cut sentences to probation and four of the six teachers were reinstated.

cases.title: South Korea — runaway children in commercial sex; police officer convicted (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Entertainment establishments, escort services, chat-room operators
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit South Korean women and children, including runaways, in bars, nightclubs and internet-advertised escort services, and chat-room operators coerce children with compromising images into producing sexual material. A court convicted a local police officer in a 2022 case involving alleged complicity in trafficking-related crimes and sentenced him to five years; another officer was acquitted.
cases.cover_up: NGOs previously reported some local police sexually exploited children; one officer was convicted (bribery, secrecy violations) and another acquitted.

cases.title: Mongolia — girls sex-trafficked in Ulaanbaatar hotels and karaoke bars (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers in hotels, massage parlours, karaoke clubs
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says women and girls are sex-trafficked in Mongolian hotels, massage parlours, illegal brothels, bars and karaoke clubs, mostly in Ulaanbaatar, provincial centres and border areas, sometimes facilitated by a lack of police enforcement; traffickers use online platforms to groom and blackmail children; and children taken abroad for competitions have instead been put to work, e.g. as horse jockeys.
cases.cover_up: The report says exploitation is sometimes facilitated by lack of police enforcement; some families are complicit.

cases.title: South Korea school deepfake crisis on Telegram (2024)
cases.who: Telegram group chats creating sexual deepfakes of classmates and teachers
cases.what: In August 2024 a journalist's reporting revealed Telegram chatrooms, some dedicated to specific high schools and middle schools, where users made and shared sexual deepfakes of female students, teachers and others; one room for pupils at a single school had more than 2,000 members. Within a week activists had identified more than 500 schools and universities as targets. Police said they had handled more than 800 deepfake sex crime cases in 2024 by late September, against 156 in all of 2021, and that most victims and perpetrators were teenagers. On 26 September 2024 the National Assembly passed a bill criminalising possessing or watching sexual deepfakes; earlier that month police opened an investigation into whether Telegram was complicit.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Nth Room and Doctor's Room — Telegram sexual blackmail rings
cases.who: Telegram chatrooms 'Nth Room' (Moon Hyung-wook) and 'Doctor's Room' (Cho Ju-bin)
cases.what: Operators blackmailed women and girls into producing sexual images and videos and sold access to Telegram chatrooms; at least 10,000 people used the 'Doctor's Room' chats, some paying up to $1,200. At least 74 victims, including 16 minors, were exploited there. After petitions signed by millions, police named the operator, Cho Ju-bin, in March 2020 — the first official identity disclosure for a sex offender in South Korea — and on 26 November 2020 the Seoul Central District Court sentenced him to 40 years (reported raised to 42 years on appeal in 2021). Moon Hyung-wook, who created the original 'Nth Room' chatrooms, was sentenced to 34 years by the Andong court on 8 April 2021. The law was changed to punish possessing and viewing such material.
cases.cover_up: A man's early 112 report was reportedly not treated as credible (Wikipedia, citation needed); two university students ('Team Flame') and journalists exposed it in 2019.

cases.title: Operation Atlas — Virtual Global Taskforce P2P sweep
cases.who: Peer-to-peer distributors and producers
cases.what: Ten Virtual Global Taskforce members (Australia, Colombia, Netherlands, Switzerland, US HSI, Korea, New Zealand, Canada, UAE, UK) arrested 303 people suspected of distributing and producing abuse material and identified 106 victims, announced November 2015.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 3,263 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: Chibok schoolgirls abduction — Boko Haram. Dapchi schoolgirls abduction — ISWAP/Boko Haram. Kankara schoolboys abduction (Katsina, 2020). Nigeria — UN-verified abduction and forced marriage of children by JAS and ISWAP (2024).
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.
