patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Nigeria — cult-linked networks traffic women and girls to Europe and West African mines (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Nigerian organized trafficking networks, some linked to cult organizations/confraternities
cases.what: The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says highly organized groups, sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations or confraternities, recruit and exploit Nigerian women and girls in sex trafficking in Italy, Spain and the UK, and that networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. In the reporting year courts convicted 49 traffickers and the government identified 2,058 victims. It describes corruption and official complicity, including among officials responsible for anti-trafficking, as significant concerns.

cases.title: Nigeria — UN-verified abduction and forced marriage of children by JAS and ISWAP (2024)
cases.who: Jama'atu Ahlis Sunna Lidda'Awati Wal-Jihad (JAS/Boko Haram), ISWAP, Bakura
cases.what: The UN verified the abduction of 991 children (354 boys, 637 girls) in Nigeria in 2024 by JAS (690), ISWAP (294) and Bakura (7), most for recruitment and use. It also verified sexual violence, all involving forced marriage, against 419 children (7 boys, 412 girls) by JAS (304), ISWAP (114) and Bakura (1). In 2023 the UN had verified sexual violence against 366 children following abduction.

cases.title: Ogoshi brothers — Nigeria-based sextortion of a Michigan teenager
cases.who: Samuel and Samson Ogoshi, Lagos (convicted); Ezekiel Ejehem Robert (charged)
cases.what: Men in Lagos used hacked Instagram accounts, posing as a girl, to obtain explicit images from a 17-year-old in Michigan and demanded $1,000; he died by suicide in March 2022. A federal grand jury indicted the brothers in November 2022; they were extradited from Nigeria in August 2023. The indictment said they tried to extort more than 100 people. They pleaded guilty to conspiracy to sexually exploit teenage boys (announced 10 April 2024) and were each sentenced to 17.5 years in September 2024. A third defendant, Ezekiel Robert, appealed a Nigerian extradition order; charges against him remain pending.

cases.title: Black Axe in Palermo — 14 convicted (2018), 4 acquitted of mafia association (2019)
cases.who: Black Axe (Nigerian confraternity) cell in Palermo
cases.what: A Palermo police operation on 18 November 2016 arrested 19 alleged members of a Black Axe cell based in the Ballarò district; prosecutors said it ran debt collection, exploitation of prostitution and drug trafficking with mafia-style initiation rites. On 21 May 2018 a Palermo judge (fast-track procedure) convicted 14 Nigerians to a combined 87 years. In November 2019 the Palermo Corte d'Assise, trying five others, did not accept the mafia-association charge: four were acquitted and one was jailed for 11 years for kidnapping and sexual violence.
cases.network: Black Axe (Neo-Black Movement of Africa confraternity)

cases.title: Oba of Benin revokes trafficking 'juju' oaths (March 2018)
cases.who: Oba of Benin, Ewuare II; Edo traditional priests
cases.what: In March 2018 the Oba of Benin, Ewuare II, publicly revoked the curses that juju priests had used to bind trafficking victims to their traffickers and laid a curse on anyone involved in trafficking within his domain. Thomson Reuters Foundation reported in September 2018 that anecdotal evidence suggested trafficking had slowed, and cited UNODC that at least nine in ten Nigerian women trafficked to Europe come from Edo State.

cases.title: Nigeria — Aba 'baby farm': 32 pregnant girls freed
cases.who: Cross Foundation clinic proprietor
cases.what: In late May 2011 Abia State police raided the Cross Foundation clinic in Aba and rescued 32 pregnant girls, mostly aged 15–17, allegedly held so their babies could be sold for illegal adoption or ritual use; four babies already sold were recovered. The proprietor was arrested, according to police commissioner Bala Hassan. Nigerian police had uncovered a network of 'baby farms' posing as orphanages in Enugu in 2008, and more were found in later years (five in 2013, eight in 2015 per Makinde et al.).
cases.network: Nigerian 'baby factories' (recurring pattern, not a single organisation)

cases.title: Nigeria — Kaduna 'Islamic school' raid frees 300+ boys and men
cases.who: Imam Ahmad Bun Hambal Centre for Islamic Studies (purported Islamic school / rehabilitation centre)
cases.what: On 26 September 2019 Kaduna police raided a building signed as an Islamic studies centre and freed more than 300 boys and men, many chained and with whip scars. Some had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana; families said they were denied access. Seven people claiming to be teachers were arrested. Local media reported captives were tortured, starved and sexually abused. The raid led to further rescues from similar 'torture houses' in northern Nigeria.

cases.title: Nigeria — Lagos raid: 162 children rescued from 'baby factory' and unregistered orphanages
cases.what: In April 2018 Lagos State Commissioner for Youths and Social Development Agboola Dabiri said 100 girls and 62 boys had been rescued from a 'baby factory' and two unregistered orphanages; some had been sexually abused. The BBC noted babies from such places can be sold for adoption, child labour or trafficking, and that in 2013 17 pregnant teenagers and 11 babies were rescued from a house in Imo State.
cases.network: Nigerian 'baby factories' (recurring pattern, not a single organisation)

cases.title: Chibok schoolgirls abduction — Boko Haram
cases.who: Boko Haram (JAS)
cases.what: On the night of 14 April 2014 Boko Haram gunmen raided the dormitories of the Government Girls Secondary School in Chibok, Borno state, and loaded 276 girls onto trucks; more than 50 escaped within hours, mostly by jumping off the lorries, leaving 219 in captivity, some later found in the Sambisa Forest. Amnesty International said on the tenth anniversary in April 2024 that 82 girls remained in captivity and that 20 released girls had been forced to marry former Boko Haram fighters; in April 2015 it estimated that at least 2,000 women and girls had been abducted by the group since the start of 2014.

cases.title: Dapchi schoolgirls abduction — ISWAP/Boko Haram
cases.who: Boko Haram faction (ISWAP)
cases.what: On the evening of 19 February 2018 militants stormed Dapchi, Yobe state, and abducted girls from a boarding school; Nigeria's government said 110 schoolgirls were missing. On 21 March 2018 the government said 106 children — 104 schoolgirls, a girl who did not attend the school and a boy — had been freed, and denied paying a ransom. Five girls were reported to have died during the journey after the abduction. The only Christian girl in the group, who refused to convert, remained in captivity.

cases.title: Kankara schoolboys abduction (Katsina, 2020)
cases.who: Armed bandits; Boko Haram's Shekau claimed responsibility
cases.what: On the night of Friday 11 December 2020 heavily armed gunmen raided the all-boys Government Science Secondary School in Kankara, Katsina state, where more than 800 students lived. The military said 333 pupils were unaccounted for. In an audio message a man identifying himself as Boko Haram leader Abubakar Shekau claimed the abduction; Nigerian officials attributed it to bandits, and the BBC later described a local gang leader as the mastermind of the kidnapping of about 300 boys. The boys were freed within about a week.

cases.title: T.B. Joshua (SCOAN) — BBC investigation into abuse of disciples
cases.who: T.B. Joshua; Synagogue Church of All Nations (SCOAN)
cases.what: A BBC Africa Eye investigation published on 8 January 2024 reported corroborating testimony from more than 25 former disciples from seven countries that TB Joshua, founder of the Synagogue Church of All Nations in Lagos, had sexually assaulted and raped followers and subjected them to abuse including solitary confinement, with the most recent experiences in 2019. One woman said he first raped her when she was 17 and that she was made to have forced abortions. Joshua died in June 2021. The church did not respond to the BBC's allegations but has called previous claims unsubstantiated. No official finding. Religious figure placed here for celebrity and political influence.

cases.title: IOM: up to 80% of Nigerian women and girls arriving in Italy may be sex-trafficking victims
cases.who: Nigerian trafficking networks via Libya
cases.what: In July 2017 the International Organization for Migration said perhaps 80 per cent of Nigerian migrant women and girls arriving by sea in Italy could be sex-trafficking victims, and that its Italy office had seen an almost 600 per cent rise in potential victims over three years. IOM indicators included age (most victims 13–24) and being 'controlled' by other migrants. Thomson Reuters Foundation later cited IOM data that Nigerian female arrivals rose from 1,500 in 2014 to more than 11,000 in 2016.

cases.title: Kédougou, Senegal — sex trafficking of girls at gold-mining sites
cases.who: Trafficking networks supplying mining camps
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit women and girls as young as 12 in sex trafficking throughout Senegal's southeastern gold-mining region of Kédougou; most victims are from Nigeria, with others from Senegal, Mali, Benin, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Guinea, Sierra Leone and China. It also reports some tourists exploit children in Dakar and Saint-Louis, and to a lesser extent Cap Skirring and La Petite Côte.

cases.title: Côte d'Ivoire — girls brought to Abidjan for domestic servitude; Nigerian girls at mines (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Relatives and Nigerian trafficking networks
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says distant relatives bring girls from rural Côte d'Ivoire and other West African countries to Abidjan for school or training and then exploit them in domestic servitude, where they are vulnerable to sexual exploitation; Ivorian women and girls are sex-trafficked especially in Abidjan; and Nigerian traffickers recruit women and girls for shop jobs then exploit them in gold-mining and cocoa regions.

patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 20,864 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No national inquiry into institutional abuse found
patterns.role_note: Archdiocese ordered to disclose files on 915 accused clergy cases to journalist Juan Pablo Barrientos within 48 hours; full compliance not achieved
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)

cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. cases.title: Cartagena — 'La Madame' network exploiting girls for tourists (plea 2018)
cases.who: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ('La Madame')
cases.what: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ran a sex network from a Bocagrande apartment in Cartagena, supplying young women and minors to parties on yachts, in hotels and at beaches and sending women to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas; prosecutors seized 15 ledgers of clients and payments, and a WhatsApp group listed 200 women. cases.cover_up: At hearings she threatened to reveal the names of politicians and powerful men she said were clients (her claim, unverified).

cases.title: Colombia — Tren de Aragua sex trafficking of Venezuelan girls; webcam industry (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Tren de Aragua; ELN; webcam studios
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says Tren de Aragua and the ELN run sex-trafficking networks in Villa del Rosario, Norte de Santander, and Tren de Aragua uses Cúcuta's transport hub to move victims to Argentina, Ecuador and Peru and operates in Bogotá, Cali, Medellín and Pereira. cases.cover_up: Two complicit officials received plea-deal sentences of 7.5 years, below the statutory minimum.

cases.title: Colombia — ICBF investigation of 21 substitute (foster) homes

cases.title: Colombia — Constitutional Court orders Medellín archdiocese to release priests' files
cases.who: Archdiocese of Medellín; Salesian Inspectorate of San Luis Beltrán, Medellín
cases.what: In May 2019 journalist Juan Pablo Barrientos, author of 'Dejad que los niños vengan a mí', asked the Archdiocese of Medellín and the Salesians for the records of 43 priests, including complaints against them. After both refused, he filed tutela actions. On 3 March 2020 the Constitutional Court ruled that the information was semi-private and that the right to information prevailed, ordering the archdiocese to hand it over. In 2022 the Court agreed to review a further petition covering 915 priests who served in Medellín.
cases.cover_up: Both the archdiocese and the Salesian province refused journalist Juan Pablo Barrientos's 2019 request for the records of 43 priests, calling them private; the archdiocese appealed the first-instance ruling against it.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Dominican Republic → Poland: Fr Wojciech Gil.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

cases.title: Uganda — European Adoption Consultants bribery scheme; judges sanctioned
cases.who: European Adoption Consultants (Ohio, defunct); Ugandan lawyers and judges
cases.what: Between 2013 and 2016 the Ohio agency European Adoption Consultants arranged the adoption of more than 30 Ugandan children by US families; families were promised their children would attend school in Kampala but they were taken to an unlicensed home. On 14 August 2020 a federal indictment charged two EAC employees and Ugandan lawyer Dorah Mirembe (allegations; presumed innocent); an earlier employee, Robin Longoria, pleaded guilty in August 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials. On 17–18 August 2020 the US State Department sanctioned Ugandan judges Moses Mukiibi and Wilson Musalu Musene and lawyers Mirembe and Patrick Ecobu.
cases.cover_up: Bribes were paid to Ugandan judges and other officials to secure adoption orders.

cases.title: Poland — bishops' 2019 figures, Sekielski films and sanctions on bishops

cases.what: In March 2019 the Polish Episcopal Conference released a study reporting 382 priests accused of abusing 625 children between 1990 and mid-2018. The Sekielski brothers' documentaries 'Tell No One' (May 2019, over 23 million YouTube views) and 'Hide and Seek' (May 2020) led to Vatican investigations of bishops under Vos estis lux mundi. In June 2020 Pope Francis put the Diocese of Kalisz under an apostolic administrator and on 17 October 2020 accepted the resignation of Bishop Edward Janiak, accused in 'Hide and Seek' of failing to act against an accused priest. Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź was also investigated, and on 6 November 2020 the Vatican imposed disciplinary measures on Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz, who died ten days later.
cases.cover_up: Bishops sanctioned by the Vatican for protecting abusers: Janiak (Kalisz) ordered to resign June 2020; Głódź (Gdańsk) removed August 2020 after covering up abuse by Henryk Jankowski and Franciszek Cybula

cases.title: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski and Fr Wojciech Gil — Dominican Republic
cases.who: Apostolic Nunciature in the Dominican Republic; Archbishop Józef Wesołowski; Fr Wojciech Gil
cases.what: Polish Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, papal nuncio to the Dominican Republic from 2008, was recalled in 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, and Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation on 4 September 2013. patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: UNTAC Cambodia — growth of prostitution around peacekeepers.
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

cases.title: Cambodia — Lauryn Galindo adoption-fraud conspiracy; US moratorium 2001
cases.who: US facilitator Lauryn Galindo and associates; Cambodian officials paid by facilitators
cases.what: The US imposed a moratorium on Cambodian adoptions in late 2001 after fraudulent cases and raids by the Cambodian rights group LICADHO. Facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions for US families in 1997–2001, more than half of all Cambodian adoptions; the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for babies. In 2004 she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering in 17 cases, admitting she falsified documents that erased children's identities (she denied trafficking), and faced an 18-month sentence. Some adoptive families later found their children had living relatives.

cases.title: Cambodia — orphanages buying children to attract donations
cases.who: Private residential care institutions ('orphanages') in Cambodia
cases.what: The US State Department's 2019 Trafficking in Persons Report states: 'Some Cambodian orphanages purchase local children from economically disadvantaged families and subject them to malnutrition and unclean living conditions in their facilities for the purpose of attracting and profiting from charitable donations; some of these children are at further risk of sex trafficking and domestic servitude as a result of poor government oversight of adoption processes.' The same report links orphanages and trafficking in Nepal, Nigeria, Haiti, Sri Lanka and Moldova.
cases.cover_up: The report states 'endemic corruption aids and abets trafficking crimes'.
cases.network: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)

cases.title: UNTAC Cambodia — growth of prostitution around peacekeepers
cases.who: UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC) personnel (about 15,900 military)
cases.what: The arrival of UNTAC's roughly 22,000 personnel was followed by a sharp rise in prostitution, from an estimated 6,000 to more than 25,000 sex workers in two years, and by abuse of Cambodian women and girls; the UN did not keep thorough records of allegations at the time, so numbers rest on later academic reconstruction. The 1996 Machel study separately recorded children trafficked from Cambodia to brothels in Thailand. Child-specific findings against UNTAC personnel are not documented in the sources consulted.
cases.network: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)

cases.title: Svay Pak child brothels — 2003 raid and later decline
cases.who: Brothels in Svay Pak (mostly ethnic Vietnamese victims)
cases.what: Svay Pak, a poor fishing village on the outskirts of Phnom Penh, became notorious as a place where foreign men bought sex with children; CNN in 2017 reported girls there being sold by their families. After crackdowns by the government, police and international agencies, open street sales ended and the trade moved to more hidden venues such as massage parlours and karaoke bars. ABC News reported in 2017 that survey estimates of the share of minors among Cambodia's sex workers had fallen from nearly 35% to 1–2%.
cases.cover_up: The 22 January 2003 police raid was widely advertised in advance; almost all children had been moved and no pimps or clients were arrested. Local authorities had extorted brothel owners.

cases.title: Cambodia — child sex tourism and brothels; scam compounds (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Brothel and entertainment operators; foreign and Cambodian offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says Cambodian men and men from Australia, South Africa, the United States and other countries in Asia and Europe sexually exploit children in the tourism industry, increasingly via social media; children as young as 13 are exploited in brothels to pay family debts; and women and girls are exploited in online scam compounds.
cases.cover_up: The report says official complicity, including at senior levels, inhibited effective law enforcement.

cases.title: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery
cases.who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
cases.what: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.

cases.title: Gary Glitter (Paul Gadd) — UK, Cambodia and Vietnam cases
cases.who: Paul Gadd ('Gary Glitter', pop singer)
cases.what: Convicted in the UK in 1999 of possessing thousands of child abuse images (about 4,000; jailed four months). He was expelled from Cambodia in 2002 amid sex-crime allegations. In March 2006 a Vietnamese court convicted him of obscene acts with two girls aged 10 and 11; he spent about two and a half years in jail there. In February 2015, after Operation Yewtree, he was convicted of attempted rape, four indecent assaults and one count of sex with a girl under 13, against three girls in 1975–1980, and sentenced to 16 years. Released in February 2023, he was recalled to prison in March 2023 for breaching licence conditions.

cases.title: Operation Twisted Traveler — ICE crackdown on US offenders in Cambodia (2009)
cases.who: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement; Cambodian police
cases.what: In August 2009 three previously convicted US sex offenders arrested by Cambodian police in February — Ronald Boyajian, Erik Peeters and Jack Sporich — were returned to Los Angeles as the first defendants charged under 'Operation Twisted Traveler'. ICE head John Morton called Cambodia 'ground zero for child sex tourism'; ICE had stationed an agent in Cambodia full-time. Peeters was accused of abusing at least three Cambodian boys and Sporich of abusing a boy in Siem Reap (accusations at the time).

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children

patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

cases.title: Vietnam — Nam Dinh ring: 266 babies sold for foreign adoption
cases.who: Heads of two provincial social welfare centres; doctors and nurses at village clinics
cases.what: In September 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people, including the head of two social welfare centres and village clinic doctors and nurses, for 'abuse of power and authority'. They allegedly solicited infants from poor families and falsified documents saying the babies were abandoned; 266 babies were sent for foreign adoption from 2005 to July 2008. In April 2008 the US embassy in Hanoi had reported desertion numbers rising 17-fold or more at orphanages in 7 provinces, and Vietnam did not renew its adoption agreement with the US when it expired in September 2008.

cases.title: Vietnam — Operation Babylift (1975): not all children were orphans
cases.who: US government (Military Airlift Command); Holt International, Friends of Children of Viet Nam, Friends For All Children and other agencies
cases.what: In April 1975, as South Vietnam was falling, President Ford directed that a $2 million special foreign aid fund be used to fly 2,000 South Vietnamese orphans to the United States; Wikipedia, citing several sources, gives a total of over 3,300 children airlifted. The first flight, a C-5 cargo plane, crash-landed shortly after take-off on 4 April 1975, killing many of the children on board (78, according to US Defense Intelligence Agency figures cited by Wikipedia). A lawsuit filed against Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, the federal government and the adoption agencies argued that many of the children were not orphans and had been given up under duress during wartime; poor families sometimes placed children in orphanages without intending to give them up, and many adoption records lacked parental consent.

cases.title: Patong, Phuket — foreign bar owner sentenced to 1,073 years after raid freed six minors (2024)
cases.who: Illegal bar on Bangla Road
cases.what: A 2023 raid on an illegal bar on Bangla Road, Patong, rescued six victims of child sexual exploitation under 18. On 19 July 2024 the Phuket Provincial Court sentenced seven defendants, Thai and foreign; the prime defendant, a foreign owner, received a total of 1,073 years. Five senior Patong police were transferred after the raid. The 2025 US TIP report says children from Thailand, Burma, Cambodia and Laos are increasingly sex-trafficked in brothels, bars, karaoke lounges and hotels.
cases.cover_up: Five senior Patong police officers were transferred after the raid; the foreign owner initially fled to a neighbouring country.

cases.title: Operation Blackwrist — Thai boys abused for Tor sites
cases.who: Tor site administrators in Thailand and Australia
cases.what: INTERPOL launched Operation Blackwrist in 2017 after finding, during routine dark web monitoring, material showing the abuse of 11 boys under 13, published weekly on a subscription website with nearly 63,000 users. Bulgaria's cybercrime police, supported by Europol, took down the servers; US HSI, New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs, NCMEC and Australian police assisted. The main administrator in Thailand and a second administrator in Adelaide, Australia, were arrested in January 2018. In June 2018 a Thai court sentenced the Thai administrator to 146 years, and an associate received 36 years; on 17 May 2019 the Australian administrator was sentenced to 40 years and three months, the longest sentence ever imposed in Australia for child sex offences. INTERPOL said 50 children had been removed from harm and 9 offenders arrested in Thailand, Australia and the United States.

cases.title: Swiss bar owner jailed 16 years for abusing more than 80 boys in Pattaya and northern Thailand
cases.who: Unnamed Swiss national (72, from Lucerne) who ran a bar in Pattaya
cases.what: A Swiss man previously convicted of abusing children in Fribourg (1980) and Valais (1991) returned to Thailand in 1996 and, mainly in 2002–2013, abused more than 80 boys in Pattaya, where he ran a bar with a hotel room frequented by Europeans, and in Nong Hoi in the north; he also forced boys to perform acts with European clients. Charged in Fribourg with human trafficking, encouraging prostitution, sexual acts with children and abuse material, he was sentenced by a Swiss court on 1 March 2018 to 16 years.

cases.title: Mark Frost — 13 life terms for abuse of boys in Thailand and the UK (2017)
cases.who: Mark Frost (also known as Andrew Tracey), former teacher and scout leader
cases.what: Frost, who had held positions of trust in UK schools and scouting and first admitted an offence in 1992, abused boys from poor families in Thailand in 2011–2013, including streaming abuse by webcam to another European man. In February 2017 he was sentenced to 13 terms of life imprisonment after pleading guilty to 45 offences against boys in the UK and Thailand. The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse cited the case as one of only about eight successful UK prosecutions since 1997 for offences committed abroad. Eight Thai boys secured civil compensation in 2018.

cases.what: Published 12 May 2016 after two years' work, the study found sexual exploitation of children in travel and tourism had grown despite 20 years of effort, as international arrivals rose from 527 million to 1.135 billion a year. It found there is no typical offender: most are domestic or regional travellers and 'situational' offenders rather than Western paedophiles; the internet has opened new pathways; and conviction rates are alarmingly low. It identified the US and Canada as source countries for offenders and Europe as a source, with exploitation rising in Central and Eastern Europe.

patterns.role_note: Casa Pia (Lisbon): first report 1975, first action 2002 (27 years). A teacher reported abuse to leaders and police from 1975; police accused a caretaker in 1981 without action; diplomat Jorge Ritto had been removed as consul in Stuttgart (1969-71) after a complaint but stayed in service
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2022: Independent Commission for the Study of Sexual Abuse of Children in the Portuguese Catholic Church (Strecht), Jan 2022 - report 13 Feb 2023. 512 validated testimonies; a minimum of 4,815 victims; archives "the tip of the iceberg"
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Casa Pia — abuse of children in state care by a TV presenter, diplomat and others
cases.who: Casa Pia (state children's institution); Carlos Cruz (TV presenter); Jorge Ritto (ex-ambassador); Hugo Marçal (lawyer); Ferreira Diniz (doctor); Manuel Abrantes (Casa Pia official); Carlos Silvino (driver)
cases.what: Abuse at Casa Pia, a state institution caring for about 4,500 children, is said to have begun in the mid-1970s and came to light in 2002. After a trial that began in 2004, on 3 Sept 2010 six of seven defendants were convicted: former Casa Pia driver Carlos Silvino (18 years, after confessing to 639 charges of abusing boys or procuring them for others), TV presenter Carlos Cruz (7), doctor João Ferreira Diniz (7), retired ambassador Jorge Ritto (6y8m), lawyer Hugo Marçal (6y2m) and former Casa Pia governor Manuel Abrantes (5y9m); a woman accused of letting her house be used was acquitted. The convicted men other than Silvino denied the charges. Former minister Paulo Pedroso was detained during the investigation but was not tried.
cases.cover_up: A teacher reportedly began reporting abuse to Casa Pia leaders and police in 1975, and police accused a caretaker in 1981, without legal action. Ritto had been removed as consul in Stuttgart around 1969–71 after a complaint about an under-age boy, but stayed in the diplomatic service.

cases.title: Independent Commission — Catholic Church in Portugal
cases.who: Catholic Church in Portugal (commission set up by the bishops)
cases.what: An independent commission set up by the Portuguese church and led by child psychiatrist Pedro Strecht reported on 13 February 2023, after hearing from more than 500 survivors, that at least 4,815 children had been abused in the church since 1950. Most offences were time-barred; 25 cases were passed to prosecutors.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo — Vatican sanctions
cases.who: Salesians; Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo (Nobel Peace laureate)
cases.what: On 28 September 2022 Dutch magazine De Groene Amsterdammer reported that two men said Bishop Belo had abused them and other boys in Fatumaca and Dili, before and during his time as bishop. The next day the Vatican confirmed it had received allegations in 2019 and imposed disciplinary sanctions in 2020: limits on movement and ministry, no contact with minors and no contact with Timor-Leste. The sanctions were reinforced in 2021. Belo had left Timor in 2002 and worked in Maputo, Mozambique from 2004.
cases.cover_up: Vatican received allegations in 2019 and imposed sanctions in 2020 but did not disclose them until a magazine reported the case in 2022

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Lobos / Baby Heart (Brazil-led)
cases.who: Baby Heart and other Tor boards
cases.what: A year-long global investigation into the Tor child-abuse site 'Babyheart' and its administrator involved the UK NCA and West Midlands Police, Australian Federal Police and Queensland's Task Force Argos, Toronto Police, the Brazilian Federal Police, INTERPOL, Europol and US ICE, with nine countries listed (Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, France, Italy, Portugal, the US and the UK). Intelligence narrowed the administrator's location to Portugal, where the Portuguese Judicial Police arrested and charged him in 2017; examination of his devices identified seven victims directly related to him. INTERPOL and Portuguese police presented the case publicly on 23 January 2020. Brazil's Federal Police ran related 'Operação Lobos' phases.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 2,868 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

cases.title: Hungary — presidential pardon in Bicske children's-home cover-up case
cases.who: President Katalin Novák; Justice Minister Judit Varga; Bicske children's home
cases.what: In April 2023, ahead of a papal visit, President Katalin Novák pardoned about two dozen people, among them the former deputy director of the Bicske children's home, who had been sentenced in 2022 to three years four months for helping the home's director cover up his sexual abuse of children. The pardon became public in early February 2024 (reported by Telex on 2 Feb). After protests, Novák resigned on 10 Feb 2024, saying she had made a mistake; former justice minister Judit Varga, who countersigned the pardon, announced the same day that she was leaving public life. Prime Minister Orbán proposed a constitutional amendment barring pardons for crimes against children.
cases.cover_up: In April 2023 the president pardoned the home's former deputy director, Endre Kónya, who had been convicted of helping cover up the director's sexual abuse of children.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Europol: at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children missing in Europe (2016)
cases.who: Europol; organized crime exploiting the migrant flow
cases.what: On 31 January 2016 Europol's chief of staff Brian Donald told The Observer that at least 10,000 unaccompanied children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 5,000 of them in Italy and 1,000 in Sweden, and that Europol had evidence some had been sexually exploited. He said an entire criminal infrastructure had developed over 18 months around exploiting the migrant flow, with many arrests in Germany and Hungary. Save the Children estimated 26,000 unaccompanied children arrived in 2015.

cases.who: Tens of thousands of accounts sharing abuse material on an online service
cases.what: Begun in 2019 after an online service provider reported offenders exchanging imagery of the sadistic abuse of infants and children. cases.what: Spanish police followed Tor links to a private Skype group whose members from 14 countries exchanged abuse material; by May 2018 eight people had been arrested in France, Hungary, Italy, Spain and Canada.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Lima → Bolivia: Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

cases.who: Foreign offenders; parents; online abuse-material producers

cases.title: Manitoba Colony 'ghost rapes' — Mennonite colony, Bolivia
cases.who: Old Colony Mennonite community, Manitoba Colony
cases.what: Men from the Manitoba Mennonite Colony sprayed a drug through bedroom windows to sedate households, then broke in and raped women and girls, including small children. The attacks came to light in June 2009. In August 2011 a Bolivian court convicted the men of raping and sexually assaulting 151 women and girls; seven were sentenced to 25 years and an eighth man got 12 years for supplying the drug.
cases.cover_up: The attacks were first blamed on ghosts or demons; a 2013 investigation reported similar assaults continuing.

cases.title: La Pampa, Madre de Dios — Operación Mercurio 2019 and sex trafficking in mining camps
cases.who: Bar/brothel networks serving illegal gold-mining camps
cases.what: On 19–20 February 2019 more than 1,500 military and police began Operación Mercurio against illegal gold mining in La Pampa, in the Tambopata reserve buffer zone, under a state of emergency. Peru's Women's Minister said the worst crimes, including child sexual exploitation and child labour, had been committed there, and her ministry took in minors and women rescued from trafficking. Reporting in 2022 said police were still dismantling networks recruiting women to La Pampa bars; a 16-year-old girl previously rescued from a La Pampa trafficking band was found murdered at km 108 in April 2021.

cases.title: Fr Alfonso Pedrajas diary — Jesuits in Bolivia
cases.who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits) in Bolivia
cases.what: Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas (1943–2009) was made deputy director of the Juan XXIII boarding school in Cochabamba, Bolivia in October 1971 and became its director about three years later. His diary, published by El País on 30 April 2023, admits he abused dozens of children while teaching at schools in Latin America, mainly in Cochabamba, and estimates the number at about 85. In 1978 in Spain he spoke about the abuse to his Jesuit instructor; no process was opened and he was not removed. El País reported that at least seven provincial superiors and about ten Bolivian and Spanish clerics covered up his crimes. He died in Cochabamba in September 2009 and was never prosecuted.
cases.cover_up: Confessed to his instructor in 1978, who covered it up; El País reported seven provincial superiors and about ten Bolivian and Spanish clerics covered for him

patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: Sudan — RSF rape and sexual slavery of women and girls (UN Fact-Finding Mission 2024).
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found Middle East and North Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Sudan — RSF rape and sexual slavery of women and girls (UN Fact-Finding Mission 2024)
cases.who: Rapid Support Forces and allied militias; also some cases by Sudanese Armed Forces
cases.what: The independent international fact-finding mission for the Sudan found that rape and gang rape were widespread, mostly by men in RSF uniform and allied militias, with victims including girls as young as 8. It found the abduction and detention of women and girls for sexual purposes by the RSF amounted to sexual slavery. The UN Secretary-General verified sexual violence against 114 girls in 2023 (RSF 57) and 74 children in 2024 (RSF 54, RSF-affiliated militia 9) and listed the RSF for rape and abduction of children.

cases.title: Chad — sexual violence against girls by the Chadian National Army (UN verified 2022)
cases.who: Chadian National Army
cases.what: The UN verified rape and other sexual violence against three girls by the Chadian National Army in Lac Province in 2022, and in Sudan attributed 4 of 35 cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 to the Chadian National Army. In the Lake Chad basin it verified the abduction of 191 children in Lac Province and Diffa.

cases.title: Ethiopia — girls trafficked to Djibouti, Sudan and Saudi Arabia (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers and begging rings
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Ethiopian women and children in forced begging, sometimes via organized begging rings, in Saudi Arabia, and exploit Ethiopian girls in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in neighbouring countries, particularly Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes using drugs for control. Reports of official complicity continued.

cases.title: Chad — Zoé's Ark tries to fly 103 children to France (convicted 2007)
cases.who: French charity L'Arche de Zoé (founder Éric Breteau)
cases.what: In October 2007 members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were detained in Chad as they tried to fly 103 children to France; the charity said they were orphans from Sudan's Darfur region, but authorities found most were from Chad and not orphans. On 26 December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children and sentenced them to eight years' forced labour, and ordered each to pay €60,000 to each of the 103 children; a Chadian and a Sudanese defendant got four years and two Chadians were acquitted. The six were transferred to France, and Chad's President Idriss Déby pardoned them at the end of March 2008.

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)

Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

cases.what: The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says highly organized groups, sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations or confraternities, recruit and exploit Nigerian women and girls in sex trafficking in Italy, Spain and the UK, and that networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. In the reporting year courts convicted 49 traffickers and the government identified 2,058 victims. cases.title: Nigeria — Kaduna 'Islamic school' raid frees 300+ boys and men
cases.who: Imam Ahmad Bun Hambal Centre for Islamic Studies (purported Islamic school / rehabilitation centre)
cases.what: On 26 September 2019 Kaduna police raided a building signed as an Islamic studies centre and freed more than 300 boys and men, many chained and with whip scars. Some had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana; families said they were denied access. Seven people claiming to be teachers were arrested. Local media reported captives were tortured, starved and sexually abused. The raid led to further rescues from similar 'torture houses' in northern Nigeria.

cases.title: Kédougou, Senegal — sex trafficking of girls at gold-mining sites
cases.who: Trafficking networks supplying mining camps
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit women and girls as young as 12 in sex trafficking throughout Senegal's southeastern gold-mining region of Kédougou; most victims are from Nigeria, with others from Senegal, Mali, Benin, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Guinea, Sierra Leone and China. cases.title: Al Hassan (Ansar Eddine, Timbuktu) — ICC: convicted of torture/persecution; acquitted of rape and sexual slavery
cases.who: Ansar Eddine / AQIM Islamic police in Timbuktu
cases.what: On 26 June 2024 the ICC convicted Al Hassan Ag Abdoul Aziz of crimes against humanity and war crimes including torture and persecution in Timbuktu, but acquitted him of the war crimes of rape and sexual slavery (charges that included forced marriages of women and girls). patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2025: prosecution: Indonesian police bust ring selling babies to Singapore; 13 arrests (July)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away

patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Indonesia — child sexual exploitation in the Riau Islands and 'contract marriages' in Puncak (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Foreign offenders; brokers of 'contract marriages'
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says extraterritorial child sexual exploitation is prevalent in the Riau Islands bordering Singapore, and women and girls are coerced into commercial sex notably in Batam. cases.cover_up: The report says the government tacitly accepted 'contract marriages'; corruption and complicity significantly impeded efforts.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: AMISOM bases, Mogadishu — rape and sexual exploitation (HRW 2014).
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: Somalia — Al-Shabaab abduction and sexual violence against children (UN verified 2024).
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

cases.title: AMISOM bases, Mogadishu — rape and sexual exploitation (HRW 2014)
cases.who: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) Ugandan and Burundian contingents
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's report of 8 September 2014, based on 50 interviews including 21 survivors, documented 10 incidents of sexual abuse, including rape and sexual assault, and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by African Union (AMISOM) soldiers, mainly Ugandan personnel at and around AMISOM's headquarters and Burundian personnel at their base in Mogadishu. Four rape cases and one sexual assault involved girls under 18; the youngest was a 12-year-old allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier near Baidoa in May 2013. patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 5,275 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (2% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

cases.title: Cartagena — 'La Madame' network exploiting girls for tourists (plea 2018)
cases.who: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ('La Madame')
cases.what: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ran a sex network from a Bocagrande apartment in Cartagena, supplying young women and minors to parties on yachts, in hotels and at beaches and sending women to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas; prosecutors seized 15 ledgers of clients and payments, and a WhatsApp group listed 200 women. cases.who: Private and NGO shelters (albergues) under the Secretaría de Niñez, Adolescencia y Familia (Senniaf)
cases.what: A National Assembly subcommission report in early February 2021 found cases of abuse in shelters for children at social risk. By March 2021 the Public Ministry had opened 18 criminal investigations, inspected 57 shelters, interviewed about 280 children and identified 20 victims, who were moved; five people had been charged with offences including child mistreatment, embezzlement and sexual offences. The Ombudsman found irregularities in 34% of 52 shelters inspected.
cases.cover_up: The Ombudsman found 70% of 44 shelters inspected lacked suitable staff and that Senniaf did little follow-up.

cases.what: On 23 October 2024 Panama's National Police and Public Ministry carried out 'Operación Roblox' in Puerto Caimito, La Chorrera district, arresting a man accused of illicit contact with minors through the Roblox gaming platform and of threatening them to demand child sexual abuse material. patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: West Africa 'sex for aid' — UNHCR/Save the Children report and OIOS investigation
cases.who: Aid workers (UN agencies, national and international NGOs), peacekeepers and community leaders
cases.what: A joint UNHCR and Save the Children UK mission reported in early 2002 that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by employees of NGOs, UNHCR and other UN bodies, and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services then fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10, including the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a Guinean camp and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou; one substantiated case involved a peacekeeper, who was repatriated. OIOS (October 2002) found no allegation against a UN staff member substantiated and said it found no evidence of 'widespread' abuse; Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think it was wrong.

A 2007 UNICEF/Holt International report found many children entered the adoption pipeline through fraud, including false promises to birth parents, and the UN Mission found unaccredited for-profit orphanages. Canada placed a moratorium on Liberian adoptions.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Australia → Fiji: Salesian Julian Fox; Australia / New Zealand → Fiji: transferred clergy.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit children in sex trafficking, including by foreign offenders ('extraterritorial sexual exploitation'), and in forced labour and domestic servitude in Zanzibar, and that women and girls from the mainland are brought to Zanzibar with false promises. Child sex trafficking also occurs in Arusha, Dar es Salaam, Dodoma, Mbeya and Mwanza.
cases.cover_up: The report says the government did not adequately address corruption and official complicity.

cases.title: St Michael's School, Soni — Rosminian priests
cases.who: Institute of Charity (Rosminians); English priest Kit Cunningham and three others
cases.what: In the 1960s four Rosminian priests, including English priest Kit Cunningham, physically and sexually abused boys at St Michael's boarding school in Soni, Tanganyika (now Tanzania). The order openly acknowledged the crimes of the four priests but in 2010 refused to pay compensation; Cunningham died in December 2010. The abuse became public in the BBC documentary 'Abused: Breaking the Silence', broadcast on 21 June 2011. A group of 22 former Soni pupils pursued a compensation claim, and former pupils of Soni and the order's Grace Dieu school in Leicestershire announced they would sue.
cases.cover_up: The order knew of Cunningham's abuse before his death in 2010; it became public only through a BBC documentary in June 2011

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Cameroon — sexual violence against girls by armed forces and JAS (UN verified 2023).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Cameroon — sexual violence against girls by armed forces and JAS (UN verified 2023)
cases.who: Cameroon Armed Forces; JAS; unidentified perpetrators
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 17 girls in Cameroon in 2023, 10 attributed to the Cameroon Armed Forces, 6 to unidentified perpetrators and 1 to JAS. In 2024 it verified sexual violence against 6 girls (1 by the armed forces) and the abduction of 50 children.

cases.title: Yemen — sexual violence against children by government-affiliated forces and Houthis (UN verified)
cases.who: Yemen Armed Forces and affiliated forces (police, Security Belt, Amaliqah); Houthis
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 24 children (8 boys, 16 girls) in Yemen in 2023, 20 attributed to the Yemen Armed Forces and affiliated forces (Yemen Armed Forces 9, Yemeni police 4). cases.title: Jordan and Türkiye — Syrian refugee girls in forced marriages and sex trafficking (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Families and brokers arranging unofficial marriages
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says Syrian girls in Türkiye — which hosted about 2.9 million displaced Syrians — are forced into marriages in unofficial religious ceremonies, particularly in poor rural regions, and then subjected to domestic servitude and sex trafficking. In Jordan, Syrian refugee women and girls have been sold into forced marriages, and in 2022 authorities investigated a mother for allegedly exploiting her two daughters with foreign tourists.
cases.cover_up: Türkiye: no investigations of complicit officials reported, though corruption and complicity remained significant concerns.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 4,289 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

cases.title: Thailand — 'Baby 101' surrogate baby-breeding operation
cases.who: Baby 101 company
cases.what: In February 2011 Thai police freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, held in two Bangkok houses with passports confiscated by a company called Baby 101 that took orders from childless couples for newborns. A Taiwanese woman said to run the operation was charged with human trafficking; four said they had been tricked, and the health minister said some appeared to have been raped.
